body.x: Of everything agreed at a nikah, the mahr is the element most often misunderstood by the very people signing for it. It is described as a price, a penalty, a formality, a bargaining chip — it is none of these. The Quran presents it as a gift given to the woman herself, and in the marriage contract it is her exclusive, enforceable right. This guide explains what mahr is, how the prompt and deferred portions work, how families actually go about choosing a figure, and the misunderstandings worth clearing away before the conversation begins. On points where marjas rule differently, check with your own — this is an explanation, not a fatwa.
What mahr is, and whose it is

Mahr is the bridal gift specified in the marriage contract, given by the husband to the wife. Three facts about it are not matters of opinion. First, it belongs to the wife alone — not to her father, not to her family, not jointly to the couple. If her family receives it, they hold it for her. Second, it is her right by the contract itself: once the nikah is recited with a specified mahr, the mahr is a debt owed to her, not a gesture the husband may make or withhold depending on goodwill. Third, nobody may take it back or pressure her to surrender it. A wife may, of her own free will, gift part of her mahr to her husband — the Quran contemplates exactly that willing generosity — but a forgiveness extracted by embarrassment, family pressure or emotional leverage is a contradiction of what mahr is for. Its purpose is dignity: the marriage begins with the husband honouring the wife with something that is hers before it is anything else.
Prompt and deferred: the two portions

In practice the mahr is usually divided into two portions. The prompt portion (mu'ajjal) is payable at or around the nikah itself, or whenever the wife asks for it — it is hers immediately. The deferred portion (mu'akhkhar) is postponed to a later point specified by the contract's terms and the applicable rulings — classically it falls due if the marriage ends, though a wife's right in it is real from the day of the contract, not created by divorce. Families sometimes misunderstand the deferred portion as a kind of divorce fine. It is not a penalty and was not designed as one: it is simply her property, scheduled later, in the same way that the prompt portion is her property scheduled now. Both portions together make up the single mahr recorded in the nikah nama, and the split between them is part of what the two families agree.

There is no standard amount, and anyone who quotes you an average is inventing it. Real practice spans an enormous range, and all of it can be honourable. Some couples set a deliberately symbolic mahr — a modest sum, a copy of the Quran, or something of personal meaning — because they want the marriage to begin in ease rather than obligation. Some families choose gold, so the mahr holds its value physically in the wife's hands. Some set a substantial financial figure, particularly where the deferred portion is intended as the wife's long-term security. Others include something experiential or devotional, such as funding the wife's Hajj or ziyarat, sometimes alongside a monetary amount. Islamic teaching consistently discourages making mahr excessive to the point of burden or display; the recurring counsel of scholars is that a marriage weighed down at the start by a competitive mahr has begun with the wrong emphasis. The right figure is the one both families can state aloud without resentment — meaningful enough to honour the wife, light enough not to shadow the marriage.

Because mahr sits where money meets honour, the conversation about it goes wrong in predictable ways: it is raised too late, conducted like a negotiation over a purchase, or used by either side as a test of the other's worth. The families who handle it well tend to do a few things consistently. They settle it early, before invitations and emotions make every question public. They let elders or a trusted intermediary open it, so the couple are not haggling with each other. They speak of it as the wife's right being honoured, never as the price of the bride — the groom's family is not buying anyone, and the bride's family is not selling. And once agreed, they write it down and do not reopen it at the ceremony. A useful test: the figure should be one you could explain calmly to the couple themselves in ten years' time.
Mahr in the contract: why the writing matters

Mahr is not a side agreement; it is a term of the contract, recited in the aqd and recorded in the nikah nama with its prompt and deferred split. This is why the standard advice is to specify it clearly rather than leave it open. Where a permanent marriage is contracted without a mahr being specified, Shia fiqh does not simply leave the wife with nothing — the concept of mahr al-mithl, the mahr customary for a woman of her standing, exists precisely for such cases — but an unspecified mahr invites dispute about what is owed, and dispute is the opposite of what the contract is for. Write the amount in words and figures, state the split, and if any part is paid at the ceremony itself, note that too. Precision here is a kindness to everyone, including the husband, whose obligation is then as clear as the wife's right.

Mahr is not a bride price — nothing is paid to the bride's family for her
Mahr is not a divorce penalty — the deferred portion is her property from the day of the contract
A small mahr is not a cheap marriage — symbolism chosen freely honours both sides
A large mahr is not a guarantee of security or commitment — it is a debt, and debts can be disputed like any other
The wife cannot be pressed to forgive her mahr — a waiver given under pressure betrays its purpose
Mahr is not the husband's favour — it is the wife's right, owed as a matter of contract

Mahr is one of the nikah's most graceful mechanisms: a right given to the wife when the marriage begins, recorded in writing, and hers to keep, spend, save or give as she alone decides. Agree it early, state it proudly, and write it clearly.
